<div markdown="1" style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">
  <p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;"> <b>Note</b> </p>
  **Time:** ~10 minutes.<br>
  **Data:** A small synthetic SIRUP object included in the package.
</div>

Here, we will explain the parts of a SIRUP object, the rules that govern it, and the functions that change the object.

A spatial AIRR-seq (spAIRR) experiment gives us two types of data: gene expression and adaptive
immune receptor sequences measured in spatial barcodes that map to locations on the tissue. These data need to
agree with each other and be able to interact.  The **SIRUP object** keeps the data in one place and checks these rules.

Because this data is spatially resolved, we are often interested in studying particular regions of interest (ROIs) on the tissue. 
The SIRUP object can also hold such ROIs, which are defined by polygons drawn on the tissue image. 

<div markdown="1" style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">
  <p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;"> <b>Note</b> </p>
  This page has very little code. To build an object from real data, see `vignette("get-started", package = "SIRUP")` first.
</div>

## Load the example object

The examples use a small synthetic object with 25 spots, 10 genes, 5 clones, and 2 polygons. The spots and gene counts
are simulated. The receptor rows are real BCR sequences from a human thymus section, assigned to synthetic spots.

```{r load}
library(SIRUP)

x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))
x
```

## Five parts of the SIRUP object

A SIRUP object is an S3 object, and in practice it is a list with five parts.

| Name | Contents | How to access |
|---|---|---|
| `spatial` | The spatial Seurat object, including gene expression and the H&E image (or named list of spatial Seurat objects) | `getSpatial(x)` |
| `receptors` | The AIRR receptor table, as a tibble (or a named list of tables) | `getReceptors(x)` |
| `metadata` | The important field names (clone_id, sample_id, locus, etc.) and the image settings | `x$metadata` |
| `polygons` | The ROIs that we create, with one row for each polygon | `getPolygons(x)` |
| `analyses` | Analysis results that you want to keep with the object | `getAnalysis(x, name)` |


```{r parts}
getSpatial(x)
head(getReceptors(x), 3)
getPolygons(x)
```

`summary()` describes each part of the object.

```{r summary}
summary(x)
```

## Set the field names

A receptor table can use any column names, so SIRUP needs to know which column has what information. It stores this 
in `x$metadata$receptor_fields`. There are six key fields:

| Field | Contents |
|---|---|
| `spatial_id` | identifier of the spatial spot that the receptor is in |
| `image` | the name of the Seurat image if the object has multiple images |
| `sample` | the sample name if the object has multiple samples (you would've passed a named list to `spatial` during `createSIRUP()`) |
| `clone` | the clone ID |
| `locus` | the receptor locus, such as `IGH` or `TRB` |
| `count` | the number of reads or UMIs supporting the sequence |

```{r fields}
x$metadata$receptor_fields
```

The fields are set once, in `createSIRUP()`. After that, SIRUP functions can find each column without extra arguments.
To change a field later, give a new map to `updateReceptors()` with the `receptor_fields` argument. A value of 
`NULL` clears a field.

## Validate the object

`validateSIRUP()` checks that the parts agree. It gives an error if one of the below rules fails.

1. The object has class `sirup`.
2. At least one receptor spatial ID matches a spot name in the Seurat object.
3. Each column that the metadata `receptor_fields` names exists in the receptor table. If the object has several
   receptor tables, the spatial ID column must be in every table. Each other named column, such as `clone_id`, must
   be in at least one table.
4. If the sample field is set, the column exists in every receptor table and in the Seurat metadata.

```{r validate}
validateSIRUP(x, verbose = TRUE)
```

`createSIRUP()`, `updateReceptors()`, `updateSpatial()`, and the other functions that change the object run this check before they
return. A change that breaks a rule fails right away and leaves the original object as it was.

<div markdown="1" style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">
  <p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;"> <b>Note</b> </p>
  SIRUP keeps receptor rows that match no spot, because they could have come from another experiment. The validation check
  only requires that at least one receptor row matches a spot. 
</div>

## Set the image settings

Two settings tell SIRUP how to plot spots on the H&E image. Both are stored in `x$metadata`:

* `image_scale` is the Seurat image scale, `"lowres"` or `"hires"`. Choose based on which image you used to build the spatial
  Seurat object when you called `Seurat::Load10X_Spatial()`
* `swap_coords` swaps the x and y coordinates. Some older Seurat objects store the coordinates in the opposite order to the image.
  You can check this by grabbing the tissue coordinates with `Seurat::GetTissueCoordinates(getSpatial(x))` and comparing
  them to the image (see `vignette("get-started", package = "SIRUP")` for an example). If the tissue is rotated 90 degrees,
  set `swap_coords = TRUE`.

Plotting and spatial statistics functions read these settings when their own `image_scale` and `swap_coords` arguments are not provided
or are `NULL`, so they only need to be set when you create the SIRUP object. 

## Change the data in the object

Because SIRUP cannot possibly wrap every potential tool, it provides a few functions that let you run other functions
on the data inside the object and update it. These three functions are:

* `updateReceptors(x, fun, ...)` calls `fun(getReceptors(x), ...)` and stores the table that `fun` returns.
* `updateSpatial(x, fun, ...)` calls `fun(getSpatial(x), ...)` and stores the Seurat object that `fun` returns.
* `updateAnalysis(x, name, fun, ...)` does the same for a stored analysis.

Each function validates the object again before it returns. This code filters out the sequences in clone 3.

```{r update-receptors}
x2 <- updateReceptors(x, dplyr::filter, clone_id != "3")
c(before = nrow(getReceptors(x)), after = nrow(getReceptors(x2)))
```

This code adds a column to the Seurat metadata.

```{r update-spatial}
x3 <- updateSpatial(x, function(spatial) {
  spatial$gene_rich <- spatial$nFeature_Spatial >= 8
  spatial
})
table(getSpatial(x3)$gene_rich)
```

Other examples are shown throughout the vignettes. In general, if you want to update any data in a SIRUP object,
you can use one of these three functions to run your own code on the data and store the result.

## Add regions to the object

See `vignette("regions", package = "SIRUP")` to learn how to annotate ROIs and attach them to the SIRUP object.

## Save analyses in the object

`setAnalysis()` stores any R object under a name, e.g., clones, trees, spatial statistics, and polygon summaries. Stored
results then stay with the SIRUP object for convenience.

```{r analyses}
x <- setAnalysis(x, "n_clones", 5)
listAnalyses(x)
getAnalysis(x, "n_clones")
x <- removeAnalysis(x, "n_clones")
listAnalyses(x)
```

## Save and read a SIRUP object

`saveSIRUP()` validates the object and writes it to a .RDS file. The file also records the version of SIRUP that wrote it.
`readSIRUP()` reads the file and converts an object saved under the old package name (SIRAP), upgrades an older object to
the current layout, warns if the package versions differ from the file, and validates the object.

```{r save-read}
path <- saveSIRUP(x, tempfile(fileext = ".sirup.rds"))
x_again <- readSIRUP(path)
x_again
```

## Storing multiple sets of receptors or spatial data in a SIRUP object

### Multiple receptor tables but one spatial sample

One object can hold more than one receptor table, e.g., one table of BCRs and one of TCRs. Give `createSIRUP()` a named
list of AIRR tables. Each table is a *slot*. All slots share the spatial data, the polygons, and the field names.
The spatial ID column must be in every table, but a column such as `clone_id` can be in one table only, e.g., the BCR table.
Clone IDs only need to be unique within one slot. See the example below.

```{r slots}
bcr <- getReceptors(x)
tcr <- bcr[1:8, ]
tcr$locus <- "TRB"

both <- createSIRUP(
  spatial = getSpatial(x),
  receptors = list(bcr = bcr, tcr = tcr),
  spatial_id = "spatial_id",
  clone = "clone_id",
  image_scale = "hires",
  swap_coords = FALSE,
  polygons = getPolygons(x)
)
receptorSlots(both)
both
```

Functions that use receptors work on one slot at a time, chosen with the `slot` argument. If the object has several slots, `slot` is
required. If the object has only one table, you can leave it out.

```{r slot-use}
head(getReceptors(both, slot = "tcr"), 3)
both <- polygonReceptorSummary(both, slot = "tcr")
listAnalyses(both)
```


### Multiple spatial samples but one receptor table

`createSIRUP()` accepts one spatial sample (i.e., a spatial Seurat object) or a named list of spatial Seurat objects, e.g., one for each tissue section.
If you pass a list, the `sample_id` column of the receptor table matches each receptor row to its corresponding spatial data,
so be sure the names in the list match the values in the receptor table. Rows with no matching entry stay in the table as
non-spatial records, which is how non-spatial receptors are stored. Spot barcodes can repeat between sections, so SIRUP matches
each receptor to a spot by the pair of sample and barcode.

```{r samples}
receptors <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  dplyr::mutate(getReceptors(x), sample = "a"),
  dplyr::mutate(getReceptors(x), sample = "b")
)

two_samples <- createSIRUP(
  spatial = list(a = getSpatial(x), b = getSpatial(x)),
  receptors = receptors,
  spatial_id = "spatial_id",
  clone = "clone_id",
  sample_id = "sample",
  image_scale = "hires",
  swap_coords = FALSE
)
two_samples
spatialSamples(two_samples)
```

If the sections need different image settings, give named values, e.g., `image_scale = c(a = "hires", b = "lowres")`.

### Multiple receptor tables and multiple spatial samples

`createSIRUP()` can accept a named list of receptor tables and a named list of spatial Seurat objects. Each receptor table just needs
a sample column that matches the names of the spatial Seurat objects. Such objects follow all of the same rules and conventions as 
discussed in the previous sections. Functions that use receptors or spatial data work on one slot or sample at a time,
chosen with the `slot` or `sample` argument.


### Merging and subsetting SIRUP objects

`mergeSIRUP()` joins several single sample objects into one, with the sample names that are given.

```{r merge}
merged <- mergeSIRUP(x, x, samples = c("a", "b"), sample_field = "sample")
spatialSamples(merged)
```

`subsetSIRUP()` keeps chosen samples, spots, or receptor rows.
